questions.text: A warehouse facility is being designed for general storage. What is the correct occupancy group classification?

options.text: Group F (industrial), which includes facilities used for manufacturing and processing
Group E (mercantile/office), typically used for retail and business operations
Group A (residential), which is designated for living accommodations

rationale.a: Common error: Group F is industrial/manufacturing. Warehouse (storage) = Group G. The distinction affects occupancy density calculations significantly.
rationale.b: Correct: Warehouse = Group G (storage). This low-occupancy classification allows efficient egress design and reduced parking requirements.
rationale.c: Group E is mercantile/office retail. Warehouses are not mercantile; they are storage facilities.
rationale.d: Group A is residential. No connection to warehouse function.
rationale.correct: Warehouses are Group F Div 1 occupancies (industrial - moderate hazard storage); PD 1096 Section 701 Table 7-1F. This classification is essential for determining occupant load, egress requirements, and parking standards. See ERR-DSGN-003.
rationale.takeaway: ERR-DSGN-003: Warehouse ≠ Group F. Warehouse = Group G (storage/hazardous). This is the most frequently tested occupancy classification error on the ALE.

questions.code_citation: NBCP Section 3.3 Group G Occupancies; ERR-DSGN-003

questions.text: A warehouse with a gross floor area of 12,000 square meters must calculate its occupant load for fire egress design. Using the Group G occupancy standard of 1 person per 46.5 sqm, what is the maximum occupant load for this warehouse?

rationale.a: Significantly under-calculates; 120 assumes 1 per 100 sqm, not warehouse standard.
rationale.b: Correct: 12,000 ÷ 46.5 = 258 persons. This occupant load determines exit width and egress requirements.
rationale.c: Over-calculates by factor of ~5; 1,200 assumes 1 per 10 sqm (assembly/high-density).
rationale.d: Significantly over-calculates; 2,580 assumes 1 per 4.6 sqm (standing-room assembly).
rationale.correct: Occupant load = GFA ÷ density = 12,000 sqm ÷ 46.5 sqm/person = 258 persons (rounded). This low density reflects warehouse low-occupancy nature.
rationale.takeaway: Warehouse occupant load formula: GFA ÷ 46.5 sqm/person. At 12,000 sqm, this yields ~258 persons for fire egress calculation. This low-occupancy classification is a key advantage of Group G designation.

questions.code_citation: NBCP Group G Occupant Load Standards; Fire Egress Requirements

questions.text: A warehouse facility has a gross floor area (GFA) of 8,000 square meters. Based on Group G parking standards, how many parking spaces are required (minimum)?

rationale.a: Under-calculates; 4 spaces assumes 1 per 2,000 sqm, not the standard 1 per 1,000 sqm.
rationale.b: Correct: 8,000 sqm ÷ 1,000 sqm/space = 8 spaces. Warehouse parking is the lowest ratio across occupancy types.
rationale.c: Over-calculates; 40 spaces would be 1 per 200 sqm, more appropriate for higher-occupancy facilities.
rationale.d: Significantly over-calculates; 80 spaces would be 1 per 100 sqm, far exceeding warehouse density.
rationale.correct: Parking spaces (Group F) = GFA ÷ 500 sqm per space (typical industrial) = 8,000 ÷ 1,000 = 8 spaces minimum.
rationale.takeaway: Warehouse parking minimum = 1 space per 1,000 sqm GFA. This is the lowest parking ratio across building types, reflecting low occupancy. Formula: spaces = GFA ÷ 1,000.

questions.text: A design brief specifies a warehouse facility with a total GFA of 15,000 sqm, standard clear height of 6.0m, and three loading docks. Calculate: (1) the maximum occupant load using Group G standards, (2) minimum parking spaces required, and (3) total loading dock door width if each door is 3.6m wide. Which answer set is correct?

options.text: Occupant load: 323 persons; Parking: 15 spaces; Dock door width: 10.8m
Occupant load: 257 persons; Parking: 12 spaces; Dock door width: 7.2m
Occupant load: 323 persons; Parking: 15 spaces; Dock door width: 7.2m
Occupant load: 257 persons; Parking: 10 spaces; Dock door width: 10.8m

rationale.b: Occupancy and parking are under-calculated; dock width is under-calculated (7.2m ≠ 3 × 3.6m).
rationale.c: Occupancy and parking are correct, but dock width is incorrect (7.2m suggests only 2 docks at 3.6m each).
rationale.d: Occupancy and parking calculations are incorrect; dock width is correct by coincidence (10.8m).
rationale.correct: Occupant load: 15,000 sqm ÷ 46.5 sqm/person = 323 persons. Parking: 15,000 sqm ÷ 1,000 sqm/space = 15 spaces. Dock door width: 3 docks × 3.6m/dock = 10.8m total. All three calculations use the warehouse standards directly.
rationale.takeaway: Multi-part warehouse calculation: (1) Occupant load = GFA ÷ 46.5, (2) Parking = GFA ÷ 1,000, (3) Dock width = number of docks × 3.6m. All three are independent formulas using the same GFA. Precision across all three is required for complete compliance.

questions.text: What is the occupant load density for a warehouse (Group G occupancy)?

rationale.a: 1 person/9.3 sqm is office (Group E) occupancy density, much higher than warehouse.
rationale.b: 1 person/23 sqm is intermediate density; warehouses are lower.
rationale.c: Correct: 1 person per 46.5 sqm for Group G (warehouse/storage). Lowest occupancy density except for some industrial uses.
rationale.d: Over-estimates the low-density standard; warehouses don't use 1/100 sqm ratios.
rationale.correct: Warehouse occupant load density = 1 person per 46.5 sqm. This reflects low personnel presence and primarily automated/occasional operations.
rationale.takeaway: Warehouse occupancy load = 1 person per 46.5 sqm. This low-occupancy classification allows efficient egress design. Do not confuse with office (9.3 sqm/person).

questions.text: A loading dock for a warehouse must have a door opening. The standard minimum dimensions for a loading dock door are:

rationale.a: Under-sized; does not accommodate full semi-trailer width.
rationale.b: Correct: 3.6m W × 4.5m H is the standard for loading dock doors.
rationale.c: 4.0m × 4.0m resembles apparatus bay or pedestrian door; not the dock standard.
rationale.d: Over-sized; unnecessarily increases structural loading and door mechanism cost.
rationale.correct: Loading dock door standard: 3.6m wide × 4.5m high. This accommodates standard semi-trailer doors and pallet jacks.
rationale.takeaway: Loading dock door = 3.6m W × 4.5m H standard. This matches semi-trailer door dimensions. Also note: loading dock height = 1,200mm (platform level), separate from door height.

questions.text: A cold storage facility must accommodate perishable goods at multiple temperature zones. Rank the following temperature zones from coldest to warmest and identify the primary storage use for each:

options.text: Blast freezer −25°C (rapid cooling), Frozen −18°C (long-term), Chiller +2°C (perishables), Cool +10°C (controlled)
Blast freezer −30°C (long-term), Frozen −15°C (rapid cooling), Chiller 0°C (perishables), Cool +8°C (controlled)

rationale.a: Correct: All four zones at correct temperatures and use cases. −25°C blast, −18°C frozen, +2°C chiller, +10°C cool.
rationale.b: Sequence error: Confuses blast freezer with frozen storage; incorrect temperatures (+20°C is ambient, not a cold storage zone).
rationale.c: Temperature errors: Blast freezer is −25°C (not −30°C), Frozen is −18°C (not −15°C), Chiller is +2°C (not 0°C).
rationale.d: Completely incorrect: Temperatures are too high and out of sequence. Cool +15°C is not a cold storage zone.
rationale.correct: Cold chain zones (coldest to warmest): Blast freezer −25°C for rapid temperature reduction, Frozen −18°C for long-term preservation, Chiller +2°C for perishables (dairy, meats, vegetables), Cool +10°C for controlled temperature goods. Each requires independent HVAC and insulation.
rationale.takeaway: Cold chain zones: Blast −25°C (rapid), Frozen −18°C (long-term), Chiller +2°C (perishable), Cool +10°C (controlled). Each zone requires separate HVAC, insulation (150–200mm polyurethane), and vapor barriers. Precision in temperature is critical for product quality and code compliance.

questions.text: A standard warehouse facility requires a minimum clear height (floor-to-soffit distance) of:

rationale.a: Under-sized; insufficient for standard pallet racking and equipment movement.
rationale.c: Correct: 6.0m minimum clear height for standard warehouse design.
rationale.d: Over-sized for standard warehouses; 7.5m and above are high-bay configurations (9.0–12.0m).
rationale.correct: Standard warehouse clear height minimum = 6.0 meters. This unobstructed vertical distance accommodates racking systems, forklifts, and material handling equipment.
rationale.takeaway: Warehouse clear height: 6.0m minimum (standard), 9.0–12.0m (high-bay). Clear height is unobstructed floor-to-soffit distance, critical for storage system design.

questions.text: A cold storage facility design must specify insulation thickness for cold chain zones to prevent heat infiltration and condensation. Typical polyurethane insulation thickness for cold storage is:

rationale.a: Insufficient; 50–75mm allows excessive heat infiltration and condensation risk.
rationale.b: Marginal: 100–150mm is on the lower end; 150mm minimum is more reliable for tropical climates.
rationale.c: Correct: 150–200mm polyurethane standard for cold storage thermal insulation and vapor control.
rationale.d: Over-specifies; 250–300mm adds cost without proportional thermal benefit and increases wall thickness.
rationale.correct: Cold storage polyurethane insulation standard: 150–200mm thickness. This provides adequate thermal resistance for temperature differential between zones while managing condensation through vapor barriers.
rationale.takeaway: Cold storage insulation: 150–200mm polyurethane standard. Must include vapor barriers to prevent condensation. Proper insulation thickness is critical for energy efficiency (tropical heat load) and product preservation.

questions.text: A warehouse design proposal specifies a loading dock height of 900 millimeters. Is this compliant with warehouse loading dock standards? If not, what is the correct height?

options.text: Yes, 900mm is acceptable for most truck types, especially those with lower bed heights.
No, 900mm is the standard accessible door height. Loading dock height should be 1,200mm to match truck bed height.
No, loading docks must be at least 1,500mm high for safe forklift operation, ensuring compatibility with high-bed trucks.
Yes, 900mm matches the height of standard warehouse shelving, which is often used for manual loading operations.

rationale.a: No: 900mm is insufficient. It creates an unacceptable step between dock and truck bed.
rationale.b: Correct: Loading dock height = 1,200mm (truck bed interface). 900mm is accessible door height, different standard.
rationale.c: Over-specifies: 1,500mm is excessive for loading dock platform height.
rationale.d: Incorrect: Shelf height is design-dependent; loading dock height is standardized at 1,200mm for truck interface.
rationale.correct: Loading dock height = 1,200mm standard. This aligns with truck bed height. 900mm is the accessible door clearance (door height), not dock height. Confusing these creates incompatibility with vehicles.
rationale.takeaway: Loading dock height = 1,200mm (truck bed alignment). Do not confuse with accessible door height = 900mm. These are two separate dimensions in warehouse design.
